config.title: Configure the experiment

target.label: What do you want to predict?
target.help: You can pick any column: we tell you what kind of prediction it would be. The app trains two-category columns (yes/no, 0/1), several-category columns (up to 20, like a plan or a region) and quantities (a price, a consumption, a duration). If there's nothing to predict, pick “No target” to group similar rows.

warnings.date: We found columns that look like dates ({cols}). This version doesn't split by time; they're ignored as predictors.

sanitation.clean: Nothing to clean up: the dataset was already tidy.
sanitation.title: We cleaned up the dataset before training:
sanitation.duplicates: Removed {count} exact duplicate rows (keeps the same row out of both training and test).

exclusion.id-column: Dropped «{column}»: a distinct value per row (an identifier or free text), no signal to generalize from.
exclusion.constant-column: Dropped «{column}»: a single value, it carries no information.

sanitation.coercion: In «{column}» we set {count} non-numeric cells to empty (the rest are numbers).

eda.title: Before training, look at these signals:
eda.possible-leak: «{column}» predicts the target almost perfectly: it could be a leak (data you wouldn't have at real prediction time). If so, remove it from your CSV and load it again.
eda.id-like: «{column}» looks like an identifier (almost one value per row): it rarely helps generalize. You can remove it from your CSV without losing anything.
eda.target-skewed: The target is heavily skewed (skewness {skew}): a few very large values carry a lot of weight. The mean absolute error (MAE) treats every miss alike; RMSE punishes misses on those large values harder.
eda.target-outliers: {share}% of the target's values sit far from the rest (beyond 3 interquartile ranges). Check whether they are data-entry mistakes before training: they can pull the model a long way.
eda.imbalance: The target is imbalanced: the minority class is {rate}% of the data. The verdict accounts for it (uses AUC).

results.title: Verdict

verdict.beatsDetail: by {delta} in {metric} — {model} vs the best baseline's {baseline}
verdict.tiesDetail: a simple model does just as well: {model} vs {baseline}. There is no extra signal to learn from these columns — adding variables related to the target usually helps more than switching models.
verdict.losesDetail: a simple model does better: {model} vs {baseline}. Your current columns don't carry enough signal about the target — try variables more related to what you want to predict.
verdict.suspiciousDetail: A perfect result almost always hides a leak, not a great model.
verdict.suspiciousClassDetail: A column separates one category from the rest almost perfectly. The figures below may be inflated even if they don't look perfect.
verdict.chosenNote: ◆ Chosen by you, not by cross-validation. If you chose it by looking at the test, this number may be optimistic.
verdict.logisticTie: The league found nothing better than the reference regression
verdict.logisticTieDetail: No model beat logistic regression in cross-validation by more than one standard error, and logistic regression is also the baseline. With these columns there is no extra signal to learn: adding variables related to the target usually helps more than changing the model.

results.testNote: The verdict metrics, the confusion matrix and the baselines are computed on the test set, never on the training set. The league table uses cross-validation inside the training set: it is for choosing.

leakage.title: Possible data leakage
leakage.finding: The column “{column}” could be a proxy for the target.
leakage.hint: Remove it and retrain to see the honest performance.
leakage.none: No obvious leakage found (this check is a help, not a guarantee).
leakage.findingClass: The column “{column}” separates the category “{class}” from the rest almost perfectly: it could be a proxy for the target.

use.title: Use your model
use.desc: Score a new CSV with this model, or save it as a file to reuse it without retraining.

export.error: The model could not be exported. Try again.
export.contents: The file contains what the model learned from your data (parameters, categories, medians) — not your raw rows. Still, treat it as a sensitive file.

verdict.beatsDetail: On average it is off by ±{model}; {baseline} is off by ±{reference}: {pct}% less error.
verdict.tiesDetail: On average it is off by ±{model}; {baseline} is off by ±{reference}: practically the same. There is no extra signal to learn from these columns — adding variables related to the target usually helps more than switching models.
verdict.losesDetail: On average it is off by ±{model}; {baseline} is off by less: ±{reference}. Your current columns don't carry enough signal about the target — try variables more related to what you want to estimate.
verdict.linearTie: The league found nothing better than the reference linear regression
verdict.linearTieDetail: No model beat linear regression in cross-validation by more than one standard error, and linear regression is also the baseline. On average it is off by ±{model}. With these columns there is no extra signal to learn: adding variables related to the target usually helps more than changing the model.
verdict.units: Figures are in the units of «{column}»: its name carries no unit the app recognizes.

regression.primaryMetric: Main metric: MAE, the average error in the target's units
regression.guide: Which one to read: MAE says how far off it is on average. RMSE punishes large errors more: if it is much larger than MAE, it misses by a lot now and then. R² says how much of the variation it explains: 1 is all of it, 0 is the same as guessing the average, and it goes negative when it does worse. MedAE is the typical error, without extreme cases weighing in.

chart.title: Estimated vs actual, on the test set
chart.label: Scatter plot of {shown} test rows: actual value on the horizontal axis, estimate on the vertical one. {inside} in every 100 land within ±{mae} of their actual value.
chart.sample: The chart shows {shown} of the {total} test rows (a fixed sample spread across the whole range). What follows uses all {total}.

residuals.title: How the errors are spread
residuals.middle: Half of the estimates are off by between {p25} and {p75}.
residuals.abs90: 9 in 10 are off by less than ±{abs90}.

median.over: The median error is {p50}: it tends to overestimate.
median.under: The median error is {p50}: it tends to underestimate.
median.none: The median error is {p50}: no clear lean to either side.

residuals.sign: Error = estimate − actual: positive means overestimating; negative, underestimating.
residuals.tableCaption: Error percentiles over the {total} test rows

regression.baselinesNote: Baselines don't compete: they measure whether the league adds anything. The median is the constant with the smallest average error; linear regression, the simplest straight line.
regression.testNote: The verdict, metrics, chart and baselines are computed on the test set, never on the training set. The league table uses cross-validation inside training: it is for choosing.

multiclass.guide: Look at balanced accuracy: for each category, the share it gets right, averaged. With {k} categories, guessing at random gives {chance}; 1.00 would mean always right. Plain accuracy can mislead when one category dominates.
multiclass.noProbabilities: This model picks the category but gives no probabilities, which is why log loss and AUC show as «—».
multiclass.topConfusion: The most frequent mix-up: rows of “{real}” the model took for “{predicted}” ({count} in the test set).
multiclass.noConfusion: On the test set, the model didn't mix up any category with another.
multiclass.testNote: The verdict, the matrix, the per-category metrics and the baselines are computed on the test set, never on the training set. The league table uses cross-validation inside training: it's for choosing; this is for believing.
multiclass.confusionHow: Each row is the real category; each column, the one the model predicted. ✓ marks the hits (the diagonal); everything else is a mix-up.

score.noProbabilities: This model decides the class but does not give a probability, so the probability column is left out. If you need to rank rows by risk, choose a model that gives one.
score.subtitleQuantity: Upload a new CSV with the columns the model knows (without the target column) and get the estimated quantity for each row. Everything happens in your browser.

score.subtitleMulticlass: Upload a new CSV with the columns the model knows (without the target column) and get the predicted category and its probability for each row. Everything happens in your browser.
score.multiclassProbabilityNote: The probability is the predicted category's: how sure the model is about that row. With several categories it can be low even when the predicted one is the most likely.
score.subtitleCluster: Upload a new CSV with the columns the grouping uses and the app assigns each row a group, with the same rule. Everything happens in your browser.
score.groupProbabilityNote: The probability is the assigned group's, according to the Gaussian mixture.

why.title: Why does it predict this way?
why.method: Permutation importance on the test set: how much the model degrades when each variable's relationship with the target is broken.
why.empty: There are no importances to show for this experiment.

direction.categorical: · the effect varies by category (there is no single direction)
direction.unclear: · no clear direction (it doesn't push consistently one way)
direction.unused: · the model doesn't rely on this variable (removing it wouldn't cost accuracy)
direction.multiclass: · with several categories there is no single direction: it can make one category more likely and another less

narration.title: In words
narration.aiIntro: Generates a plain-language explanation. Column names and aggregate figures are sent to an AI provider —NEVER your rows— and only when you press the button.
narration.loading: Generating the narrative and verifying it against the numbers…

fallback.unavailable: AI narration isn't configured in this deployment.
fallback.provider: The AI provider didn't respond. You can try again.
fallback.rejected: The AI narrative didn't pass verification against the numbers; for honesty it isn't shown. You can try again.

narration.aiNotForQuantity: AI narration only covers classification into two categories. When estimating a quantity, the reading is the standard text above, built from the same numbers.
narration.aiNotForMulticlass: AI narration only covers classification into two categories. With several categories, the reading is the standard text above, built from the same numbers.

why.legend: The bar measures how much each variable MATTERS; the line below says which way it PUSHES. A variable can matter a lot and still have no single direction — that doesn't make it irrelevant.
why.positiveClass: The model predicts the column “{target}”. The class it tries to detect (the less frequent one) is “{positive}”.

directionQuantity.positive: ▲ the higher the value, the higher «{target}»
directionQuantity.negative: ▼ the higher the value, the lower «{target}»

why.quantityNote: The model estimates the column «{target}». The bar measures how much its error (MAE) grows when that variable's link to the target is broken.
why.multiclassNote: The model classifies the column “{target}” into {count} categories. The bar measures how much balanced accuracy drops when that variable's link to the target is broken.

direction.positive: higher values make the positive class more likely

metricHelp.accuracy: share of correct calls out of the total, from 0 to 1
metricHelp.precision: of the cases it flagged as positive, how many really were, from 0 to 1
metricHelp.recall: of the real positive cases, how many it managed to catch, from 0 to 1
metricHelp.f1: balance between precision and recall, from 0 to 1
metricHelp.auc: how well it separates the two classes: 0.50 would be chance and 1.00 perfect

verdict.beats: The model is off by ±{model} on average, against ±{baseline} for the best baseline: {pct}% less error.
verdict.ties: The model is off by ±{model} on average, practically the same as the best baseline (±{baseline}); a simple rule does just as well.
verdict.loses: The model is off by ±{model} on average, more than the best baseline (±{baseline}); with these variables it adds nothing.

regression.metricNote: MAE is the average error in the target's units (0 would be always right). R² is {r2}: how much of the variation it explains, where 1 is all of it and 0 is the same as guessing the average.

direction.positive: the higher the value, the higher the target
direction.negative: the higher the value, the lower the target

regression.skewed: The target is heavily skewed (skew {skew}): a few large values weigh heavily on the error.
regression.outliers: {share}% of the target values sit far from the rest: RMSE punishes them more than MAE.

multiclass.metricNote: The primary metric here is balanced accuracy: for each category, the share it gets right, averaged. With {k} categories, guessing gives {chance} and 1.00 would be always right. Macro F1 is {f1}.
multiclass.noDirection: With several categories a variable doesn't push in a single direction: it can make one category more likely and another less likely.
multiclass.leakage: Warning: {columns} could give away a category (possible leak); these figures may be inflated.
multiclass.imbalance: The smallest category, «{class}», is {rate}% of the rows; that's why the primary metric is balanced accuracy, which weighs every category equally.

modelcard.title: Model card — {name}
modelcard.generated: Generated on {date} by Probeta DS. All computation happened in the browser: the data never left the device.

sections.explainability: Why does it predict this way?

split.rule: Preprocessing was fitted ONLY on the training set (anti-leakage by construction).
split.sizesQuantity: Training: {train} rows · Test: {test} rows (stratified by 5 target bands, seed {seed}).

method.pipeline: Imputation (median / most frequent), rare-category grouping, scaling and one-hot inside a scikit-learn Pipeline.
method.rareCategories: Rare categories grouped (learned from training only): {cols}.
method.baselines: Baselines: majority class and logistic regression.
method.baselinesQuantity: Baselines: the target's median and linear regression.
method.baselinesMulticlass: Baselines: majority class and multinomial logistic regression.

verdict.primaryQuantity: Primary metric: MAE, the average error in the target's units (lower is better); it ties when within 1% of the best baseline.
verdict.primaryMulticlass: Primary metric: balanced accuracy (for each category, the share it gets right, averaged). With {k} categories, guessing at random gives {chance}.

leakage.found: Columns suspected of leakage: {columns}. Metrics may be inflated; remove them and retrain.
leakage.none: No obvious leakage found (this check is an honest help, not a guarantee).

explainability.method: Method: permutation importance on the test set (scoring {scoring}, {repeats} repeats).
explainability.notVerified: No AI narrative is included: it was not generated or it failed the numeric verification.

limits.leakage: The leakage check catches obvious cases; it is not a guarantee.
limits.explainability: Permutation importance is global (not per-prediction) and can spread across correlated variables; the direction is univariate and does not capture interactions.
limits.dates: Date columns are detected but not used yet (no temporal split).
limits.tasks: This version does four tasks: classification into two categories, classification into several categories (up to 20), estimating a quantity and grouping rows with no target.

sanitation.duplicates: Removed {count} exact duplicate rows (prevents leakage by duplication).
sanitation.coercion: In «{column}», {count} non-numeric cells were set to empty.

selection.league: {count} models competed with {k}-fold cross-validation inside the training set (preprocessing was refit in every fold). Metric: {metric}.
selection.rule: Rule: one standard error — among the models within one standard error of the best cross-validation score ({best}), the simplest one wins.
selection.cv: Model chosen by cross-validation: {model}. The test set was opened only once, after choosing.
selection.user: ◆ Chosen by you: {model}. The cross-validation winner was {winner}. If you chose it by looking at the test scores, the verdict may be optimistic.
selection.time: League time on this device: {seconds} s.
selection.smallSample: Small sample: with fewer than {rows} rows, cross-validation scores vary a lot from one fold to another.
selection.league_one: 1 model competed with {k}-fold cross-validation inside the training set (preprocessing was refit in every fold). Metric: {metric}.

estimate.task: Task: estimating a quantity (regression). It is compared against the baseline with the smallest error: the median or linear regression.
estimate.unit: Unit: {unit}, read from the column name.
estimate.noUnit: Unit: the column name carries none the app recognizes; figures are in the units of «{column}».
estimate.targetStats: The target in training: mean {mean}, standard deviation {std}, minimum {min}, median {median}, maximum {max} (written with {count} decimals).
estimate.targetStats_one: The target in training: mean {mean}, standard deviation {std}, minimum {min}, median {median}, maximum {max} (written with 1 decimal).
estimate.errors: Errors over the {total} test rows (estimate − actual): half fall between {p25} and {p75}; 9 in 10 are off by less than ±{abs90}.
estimate.noAi: AI narration: does not apply to estimating a quantity (it only covers classification into two categories).

multiclass.confusion: Confusion matrix: each row is the real category; each column, the one the model predicted. The diagonal holds the hits.
multiclass.noAi: AI narration: not applicable. It only narrates classification into two categories; with several, the reading is the standard text.

cluster.task: Task: grouping similar rows, with no target (no test set and no verdict against a baseline).
cluster.distanceNumeric: Similarity is measured with {count} numeric columns ({columns}); the categorical ones ({categorical}) only describe the groups.
cluster.distanceAll: Similarity is measured with every column, numeric and categorical ({columns}), because there are fewer than two numeric ones.
cluster.pipeline: Imputation, scaling and one-hot inside a scikit-learn Pipeline, fitted on all rows: grouping has no split and no test (seed {seed}).
cluster.members: {count} clusterers competed, trying {min} to {max} groups: K-Means and hierarchical choose by silhouette (on a sample of {sample} rows), GMM by BIC and HDBSCAN by density.
cluster.consensus: Won by consensus: {votes} of {voters} clusterers found {k} groups, and among them {model} had the highest score.
cluster.chosen: ◆ Chosen by you: {model} (the winner of the comparison was {winner}).
cluster.noLeakage: Not applicable: grouping has no target for a column to give away.
cluster.noAi: AI narration: not applicable. It only narrates classification into two categories.

limits.cause: The groups describe your rows; they don't prove there's a cause behind them or that they'll show up in other data.
limits.silhouette: The silhouette is measured on a seeded sample of up to {sample} rows, the same for every clusterer.
limits.agglomerative: With more than {max} rows, hierarchical fits a sample and assigns the rest to the nearest group, so the browser doesn't run out of memory.

cluster.noConsensus: Won by score: there was no consensus among the {voters} clusterers (each found a different number of groups), and {model} had the highest score.

errors.title: Something doesn't add up
errors.csv-empty: The file is empty or has only a header.
errors.csv-too-large: The file exceeds the 5 MB limit.
errors.csv-ragged: Some rows have a different number of columns than the header.
errors.csv-semicolon: Your file separates columns with semicolons (;) rather than commas, so no column is recognised. This usually happens when saving from Excel in a European locale. Save it again as “CSV (comma delimited)” and upload it once more.
errors.csv-tab: Your file separates columns with tabs rather than commas, so no column is recognised. Save it again as “CSV (comma delimited)” and upload it once more.
errors.target-not-numeric: To estimate a quantity, the target has to be a number in every row, and this column has values that are not. Check it in your CSV or pick another column.
errors.target-ambiguous: This column could hold categories or a quantity, and your answer is missing. Answer the question on the «Kind of prediction» card and train again.
errors.no-features: There are no usable columns as predictors.
errors.runtime: Something went wrong while processing. Please try again.
errors.worker-dead: The compute engine stopped unexpectedly (it may have run out of memory, or its components failed to load). Try again; if it persists, try a smaller file.
errors.csv-unusable: After cleaning the dataset there's nothing left to model (all identifiers, constants, or repeated rows). Try another file.
errors.too-few-rows: There are too few examples of one of the two classes to compare models honestly: cross-validation needs at least 2 of each class in the training set. Try with more rows.
errors.too-few-rows-quantity: There are too few rows to estimate a quantity honestly: the test set needs at least 2 rows the model never saw in training. Try with more rows.
errors.contract: The engine returned a result with an unexpected shape, so we are not showing it: we would rather not show you a number we cannot verify. Try again; if it happens again, try another file.
errors.target-mixed-notation: Your target has classes written in more than one way (for example «1» and «1.0»): to train, each class must be written the same way in every row. Make them consistent in your CSV and load it again.
errors.league-empty: No model finished cross-validation cleanly (they did not converge or failed), so there is no winner that can be defended. Try more rows or other columns.
errors.too-few-rows-per-class: One of the categories has too few rows to compare models honestly: cross-validation needs at least 2 rows of each category in the training set. Try with more rows, or merge the rarest categories into one.
errors.too-few-rows-cluster: There are too few rows to cluster honestly: to tell whether the groups hold up, the app searches for them again in parts of your data, and each part needs more rows than groups. Try with more rows.
errors.target-not-usable: This column can't be used as a target: it has a single value, it's empty, or it has too many distinct values to be categories. Pick another column, or group similar rows with no target.
errors.too-few-rows-per-class-named: The category “{class}” has only {rows} row(s) in the training set, and cross-validation needs at least 2 of each category to compare models honestly. Try with more rows, or merge the rarest categories into one.

task.title: Kind of prediction

reason.few-numbers: Only {distinct} distinct numbers: they can be categories (like a 1-to-5 rating) or a quantity.
reason.too-many-categories: {distinct} distinct values: it looks like an identifier or free text, not something to predict.
reason.constant: It has a single value: there is nothing to predict.

task.blocked: The app trains this kind of prediction, but with this data models cannot be compared honestly (the reason is below).
task.notUsable: This column can't be used as a target. Pick a column with categories or with a quantity, or group similar rows with no target.

estimate.unit: You are going to estimate a quantity, in {unit}. The verdict will say how far off it is on average, in {unit}.
estimate.noUnit: You are going to estimate a quantity. Its name carries no unit the app recognizes, so figures will be given in the units of «{column}».

ask.question: Does «{column}» hold categories or a quantity?
ask.help: This data alone cannot tell; you know the column.

numerica.label: A quantity
numerica.desc: The number is estimated. The verdict says how far off it is on average, in the column's units.

multiclase.label: Categories
multiclase.desc: Each number is a category, like a 1-to-5 rating. The verdict uses balanced accuracy, which weighs every category the same.

multiclass.trainable: You're going to classify into {count} categories. The verdict uses balanced accuracy: every category weighs the same, even one with few rows.

roster.title: Who competes

cluster.title: Results · grouping

reading.exist: The groups are real: {k} stable groups
reading.existDetail: {model} separates your rows better than structureless data in the same box: score {score} against {nullScore}, a gap of {gap} (at least {gapMin} is needed). And the groups come back when {fraction}% of your rows are regrouped {runs} times: they match {ari} out of 1 (at least {ariMin} is needed).
reading.fragile: There are {k} groups, but they're fragile
reading.fragileDetail: {model} separates your rows better than structureless data (score {score} against {nullScore}, gap {gap}), but when {fraction}% of your rows are regrouped {runs} times the groups change: they match {ari} out of 1, below {ariMin}. Read them as one possible split, not as a finding.
reading.noneDetail: {model} doesn't separate your rows better than structureless data in the same box: score {score} against {nullScore}, a gap of {gap} (at least {gapMin} would be needed). The {k} groups below are one way to split the table, not a finding.

cluster.noTest: Grouping has no target: there's no test set and no verdict against a baseline. What's worth believing is this comparison with structureless data and the stability under resampling.
cluster.chosenNote: ◆ Chosen by you. The reading above is this clusterer's; the winner is still marked with ★.

sample.title: Fitted on a sample of {sample} of your {rows} rows; the rest were assigned to the nearest group.
sample.why: Why: with more than {max} rows, hierarchical clustering would need more memory than a browser can give (especially on a phone) without closing the tab. The other three clusterers use all your rows.

profiles.title: What sets the {count} groups apart
profiles.noSeparating: No column clearly separates the groups.
profiles.how: η² (numeric) and Cramér's V (categorical) run from 0 to 1: how much of that column's variation the group explains. Figures are in your columns' units.

noise.title: Outside every group
noise.desc: HDBSCAN leaves out the rows that don't fall in any dense area: it doesn't force them into a group.
noise.label: outside every group

league.title: The clusterers: {count}
league.rule: The table compares the clusterers by silhouette on a sample of {sample} rows: it's for choosing. The reading above (against structureless data and by resampling) is for believing.
league.consensus: Consensus: {votes} of {voters} clusterers found {k} groups; among them, the highest score wins.

status.no-converge: didn't converge: it doesn't vote, but you can choose it

league.scoreHow: Score = silhouette × (1 − the share outside a group): HDBSCAN doesn't win by leaving the hard rows out. Silhouette runs from −1 to 1: how much closer each row is to its own group than to the next one.
league.noConsensus: No consensus: each clusterer found a different number of groups, so the highest score wins.
league.time: Grouping took {seconds} s on this device.

labels.title: Your rows with their group
labels.desc: Download your table with one more column, “group”, holding each row's group (or “outside every group”). It's built in your browser and isn't stored anywhere else.
labels.error: The file couldn't be prepared. Try again.
labels.unavailable: The active model no longer keeps your rows' groups (it was restored after cancelling Level 2). Group again to download them.

use.title: Assign new rows
use.contents: The exported file carries the preprocessing and the assignment rule (the group centres), without any of your rows.

assign.nearest-centroid: Rule for new rows: the group whose centre is nearest.
assign.gaussian: Rule for new rows: the Gaussian mixture picks the most likely group and gives its probability.
assign.centroid-radius: Rule for new rows: the group whose centre is nearest, unless the row lands further out than that group's furthest member: then it's “outside every group”.
assign.agreement: With this rule, {pct}% of your rows land in the same group the clusterer gave them.

plan.title: Group similar rows, with no target
plan.what: There's nothing to predict: the app looks for groups of rows that resemble each other. With no target there's no test set and no verdict against a baseline; what's worth believing is the comparison with structureless data and the repeats on parts of your rows.
plan.distanceNumeric: Similarity is measured with your {count} numeric columns: {columns}.
plan.distanceAll: There are fewer than two numeric columns, so similarity is measured with all of them: {columns}.
plan.describeOnly: The categorical ones ({columns}) describe the groups but don't shape the similarity.

excluded.id-like: “{column}” is left out: it looks like an identifier.
excluded.date: “{column}” is left out: it's a date, and dates aren't used for grouping.
